subject: ela
intro: When a teacher reads a book aloud or shares information orally, good listeners ask and answer questions about what they heard. This means paying attention to key details — who the story is about, what happens, where it takes place, and why things occur. After listening, students should be able to recall details and answer questions about them. They should also be able to ask their own questions when something is unclear.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads aloud: 'A mother duck led her five ducklings to the pond. One duckling stopped to look at a butterfly. The mother quacked loudly until the duckling caught up.' 
Question: How many ducklings did the mother duck have?

steps: Listen for the number mentioned in the text.
The text says 'five ducklings.'
The answer is directly stated in the passage.
solution.answer: The mother duck had five ducklings.

items.prompt:
Same passage: 'A mother duck led her five ducklings to the pond. One duckling stopped to look at a butterfly. The mother quacked loudly until the duckling caught up.'
Question: Why did the mother duck quack loudly?

steps: This is a 'why' question — look for the reason in the text.
One duckling stopped and fell behind.
The mother quacked to call the duckling back so it would catch up with the group.
solution.answer: The mother duck quacked loudly to get the straggling duckling to catch up.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads: 'Bears eat a lot in fall to get ready for winter. They sleep for months in a den. When spring comes, they come out hungry and ready to find food.'
A student is confused about what a 'den' is. What question should she ask?

steps: When a listener does not understand a word, she should ask about it.
A good question would be: 'What is a den?'
Or more specifically: 'When you said the bears sleep in a den, what is a den?'
solution.answer: She should ask: 'What is a den?' or 'Can you explain what a den is?'

items.prompt:
A teacher reads a poem about rain:
'Pitter, patter, pitter, patter,
Rain falls down without a clatter.
Puddles form in every lane,
Nature drinks the falling rain.'
Question: What forms when the rain falls?

steps: Listen for what the poem says forms when rain falls.
The poem says 'puddles form in every lane.'
Puddles are the answer.
solution.answer: Puddles form when the rain falls.

items.prompt: After a teacher reads a story about a girl who rescues a bird, a student says, 'I didn't understand the ending — was the bird okay?' Is this a good question to ask? Why?

steps: Yes, this is a good question. The student is asking about a key detail from the text that she did not understand.
Asking about key details after a read-aloud is exactly what standard 1.SL.A.2 expects.
The question is specific (about the ending and the bird) and relevant to the story.
solution.answer: Yes, it is a good question. The student asks about a specific detail she did not understand — this shows active listening.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads: 'The lion is the king of the jungle. It has a big mane and a loud roar. Lions live in groups called prides.'
Question: What is a group of lions called?
items.hint: Listen for the specific word the text uses for a group of lions.

steps: The text directly states: 'Lions live in groups called prides.'
The answer is 'a pride'.
solution.answer: A group of lions is called a pride.

items.prompt:
Same passage: 'The lion is the king of the jungle. It has a big mane and a loud roar. Lions live in groups called prides.'
A student wants to ask a good question about this text. Which is better?
A) 'Do you like lions?'
B) 'Why is the lion called the king of the jungle?'
items.hint: A good question asks about key details in the text.

steps: Option A is a personal opinion question — not about the text content.
Option B asks about a key detail from the text ('king of the jungle') and invites deeper thinking.
Option B is the better question about the read-aloud.
solution.answer: B) 'Why is the lion called the king of the jungle?' — it asks about key information from the text.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads: 'In the winter, many birds fly south to warmer places. This is called migration. Some birds travel thousands of miles.'
Question: What is migration?

steps: Migration is defined in the text: when birds fly south to warmer places in winter.
The text also says some birds travel thousands of miles during migration.
solution.answer: Migration is when birds fly south to warmer places in the winter.

items.prompt:
After hearing a read-aloud about volcanoes, a student says, 'I heard the word lava — is that the hot rock that comes out?' Is this a good question?
A) No — she should already know.
B) Yes — she is asking to confirm her understanding of a key detail.
items.hint: Think about what makes a good question after a read-aloud.

steps: Yes, this is a good question. She is asking to clarify and confirm what she heard.
Standard 1.SL.A.2 encourages students to ask and answer questions about key details.
solution.answer: B) Yes — she is checking her understanding of a key vocabulary word from the text.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads: 'The first rainforests appeared on Earth over 300 million years ago. They are home to more than half of all plant and animal species in the world.'
Question: What fraction of all plant and animal species live in rainforests?
items.hint: Listen for the fraction or portion mentioned in the text.

steps: The text says rainforests are home to 'more than half of all plant and animal species.'
More than half = more than 50%.
solution.answer: More than half of all plant and animal species live in rainforests.
